concepts.partName: Founding and Rulers of the Bahamani Dynasty
concepts.bodyMd:
**A.D. 1347** is a landmark year in South Indian history — Allauddin Hassan Bahaman Shah established an independent Muslim kingdom in the Deccan in this year, ruling from Gulbarga as his capital. This was the first Muslim rule established in South India, and under successive Muslim rulers the Deccan made steady progress. The Bahamani kingdom lasted from **A.D. 1347 to 1526**, and the dynasty served the Deccan by establishing a stable and extensive empire, introducing many administrative reforms along the way.

The important rulers of the Bahamani dynasty, in order:

| Ruler | Reign |
|---|---|
| Allauddin Hassan Bahaman Shah | A.D. 1347 – 1358 |
| Muhammad Shah Bahamani | A.D. 1358 – 1375 |
| Mujahid Shah Bahamani | A.D. 1375 – 1378 |
| Mohammad Shah II Bahamani | A.D. 1375 – 1397 |
| Feroz Shah Bahamani | A.D. 1397 – 1422 |
| Ahammada Shah Vali Bahamani | A.D. 1422 – 1436 |
| Allauddin Shah II Bahamani | A.D. 1436 – 1457 |
| Nizam Shah Bahamani | A.D. 1461 – 1463 |
| Mohammad Shah III Bahamani | A.D. 1463 – 1482 |
| Mohammad Shah Bahamani | A.D. 1482 – 1518 |
| Kareemulla (Kalimulla) | Nominal ruler for 3 years; died **A.D. 1527** |

In all, the Bahamani kingdom was ruled by **17 sultans over 182 years**. Of these, five were murdered, two died amid disputes/troubles, three were deposed, and two were blinded — a record that reflects how turbulent the dynasty's internal politics were even as it fought its long external contest with Vijayanagara.

### Background — Two Kingdoms Rise Against Delhi

The Bahamani kingdom and the Vijayanagara kingdom were the two independent states that emerged in opposition to the imperial power of the Delhi Sultanate. Vijayanagara was founded at Hampi in **1336**, and the Bahamani kingdom was founded at Gulbarga in **1347** (Gulbarga was, at that later time, a district of the Nizam's state).

With the Delhi Sultanate weakening, the Amirs of the Deccan organised themselves and revolted against Muhammad bin Tughlaq, electing an elderly leader, Ismail Mukh, as their chief. Unable to bear the burden of rule, this elderly Amir passed authority to a younger man, **Hasan Ali**. On **3 August 1347**, this Hasan established the Bahamani dynasty under the title **Muzaffar Allauddin Ahmad Hasan Gangu**. The entire Deccan became independent within Muhammad bin Tughlaq's own lifetime.

### Allauddin Hasan Gangu (1347–58)

As soon as he gained power, Allauddin Ahmad Shah made Gulbarga his capital and renamed it **Hasanabad**. The Andhra ruler **Musunuri Kapaya Nayaka** had helped in the establishment of his kingdom — though it was Kapaya Nayaka who was the recognised power in the region before Hasan's rise.

Hasan Gangu began claiming, as heir to the Delhi Sultanate's authority over the south, rights over the whole Deccan. His ill conduct caused Kapaya Nayaka — already caught between the Reddy kings on one side and the Padma Nayakas on the other — great difficulty, and hostility between Hasan and the Hindu kings grew steadily. Hasan attacked Warangal and defeated Kapaya Nayaka, who paid tribute in elephants and wealth to make peace. Not satisfied with this, Hasan attacked Warangal twice more, plundering the villages along the way and destroying temples.

Unable to conquer coastal Andhra, Hasan instead occupied **Bidar and Malkhed**. He died in **1358**. By then his kingdom extended north from the Ganga to the Tungabhadra in the south, and from Daulatabad in the west to Bhuvanagiri in the east. He divided his kingdom into four Tarafs — **Gulbarga, Daulatabad, Bidar, and Berar** — and appointed capable governors to administer them.

### Muhammad Shah I

After Allauddin Hasan, his elder son **Muhammad Shah** succeeded to the kingdom. He was a courageous and formidable — indeed a very cruel — ruler. He attacked Warangal and forced a harsh treaty upon Kapaya Nayaka. Breaking his own word, Muhammad Shah had Kapaya Nayaka's son, **Vinayaka Deva**, killed by having his tongue thrown into burning coals — a brutal act that plunged Kapaya Nayaka into grief.

Kapaya Nayaka sought justice from the Delhi Sultan, Firoz Tughlaq, for the wrong done to him, but the self-interested Tughlaq gave him no redress; nor did Vijayanagara offer any help. Left entirely without support, the helpless Kapaya Nayaka was finally forced to make peace with the Bahamani Sultan by paying **33 lakh in cash, 300 elephants, and 200 horses** — after which only the name of the kingdom remained to him.

Muhammad Shah was an extremely cruel ruler. He invaded Vijayanagara territory and devastated the region between the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers by every possible means. Professor Sherwani recorded that his court was home to renowned Ulemas. Muhammad Shah died in **1375**.

### Mujahid Shah and Dawood's Brief Usurpation

After Muhammad Shah I, **Mujahid Shah** came to the throne. He fought wars with Bukka Raya over the Krishna–Tungabhadra doab and was defeated twice. Disgraced by this, Mujahid Shah was murdered by a man named **Dawood**, who then seized the kingdom; Mujahid Shah left no heir.

Two factions then contended for the kingdom — one backing Dawood, the other backing Allauddin's younger son. Dawood was defeated in this struggle, and while he was reciting his Namaz, a slave killed him. Dawood's rule lasted only **35 days**.

### Muhammad Shah II (1378–1397)

It was the second Muhammad Shah who safeguarded the prestige of the Bahamani kingdom. Peace-loving, devout, and sympathetic, he regarded the protection of his subjects as his duty. During his reign the Deccan suffered a terrible famine, and he arranged for grain to be brought in from the Malwa and Gujarat regions on ten thousand bullocks — though even this proved insufficient. He did not neglect his Hindu subjects either.

Much of the credit for his victories belongs to his minister **Saif Uddin**, who served as minister across the reigns of five sultans and earned a reputation as a capable administrator. Muhammad Shah II established free schools (paathshalas) in the leading towns of Gulbarga, Bidar, Elichpur, Kandahar, and Daulatabad — though these were not secular schools, as entry was reserved for Muslims only, and famine relief from the state likewise reached only Muslim subjects. He gave special donations to the poor, and — taking advantage of this generosity — many people falsely feigned blindness or poverty to obtain government benefits.

Muhammad Shah II ruled for **19 years, 5 months, and 21 days**. After him his eldest son **Ghiyasuddin** ruled for just 1 month and 22 days, followed by Muhammad Shah's younger son **Shamsuddin**, who ruled for only 7 days. The kingdom then passed to Allauddin Hasan's grandson, **Firoz Shah**.

### Firoz Shah

Firoz Shah was a capable ruler at first, but before long he turned to self-indulgence, keeping as many as eight hundred women in his harem each day. In **1389**, the grandson of the second Bukka Raya attacked Raichur in an attempt to win independence. Unable to win by fair means, Firoz Shah resorted to treachery and had the Raya's son killed. In retaliation, the returning Vijayanagara army massacred the Bahamani kingdom's Hindu subjects.

In a war fought in **1420**, Firoz Shah suffered defeat, and the humiliation left him bedridden. Having ruled for 25 years, Firoz Shah died in **1422**. The rulers who came after him were not his equal in capability.

### Ahmad Shah (1422–1433)

Ahmad Shah, who succeeded Firoz Shah, ruled from 1422 to 1433. He fought a war with the Vijayanagara kingdom and won Kolhapur as part of a territorial settlement; in this fighting some 20,000 Hindu and Muslim soldiers alike were massacred. Ahmad Shah moved the capital city from Gulbarga to **Bidar** — both cities were, at a later time, part of the Nizam's dominion.

### Allauddin Bahaman Shah II (from 1436)

Taking power in **1436**, the second Allauddin Bahaman Shah ruled for 23 years. He conquered the Konkan region, defeating the Hindu ruler of Sangameshwar and marrying his daughter. Though a patron of Islam, he built many schools and hospitals in Bidar, and issued prohibition orders against intoxicants. He arranged allowances for blind beggars and put them to work cleaning the streets, decreeing banishment from the kingdom for those who refused to work. He fought once with Vijayanagara and won, and fought again and lost; unable to bear the grief of that defeat, he became given to excessive drinking and died of it.

### Humayun Shah "Zalim" (the Cruel)

**Humayun Shah**, eldest son of Allauddin Ahmad Shah, committed many cruel acts even while he was crown prince, striking fear into the Amirs. Their efforts to keep him from the throne failed, and once in power he had those Amirs executed.

No ruler in Deccan history matched Humayun Shah's cruelty. Those who opposed him were tied by their feet to elephants and dragged mercilessly through the streets; some were thrown alive into wells; some were fed to hungry tigers — and he would laugh with demonic delight while watching such acts. On the night after a wedding, every new bride in the kingdom was made to be presented to satisfy his lust, and the anguished cries of the people rose to the sky.

One day, while he lay in a drunken, deep sleep, his own mistress struck him repeatedly on the head and killed this menace to the world. Humayun Shah's reign lasted **3 years and 6 months**.

### Nizam Shah and Muhammad Shah III

After Humayun Shah, **Nizam Shah Bahamani** took the throne as an eight-year-old boy. After some time, his brother, known as "Mudo" **Muhammad Shah (III)**, ascended the throne in **1463**.

### The End of the Dynasty

After Mahmud Gavan's murder (see below), the kingdom's foundations were shaken; self-interested Amirs seized power for themselves, and the Sultan, on learning the truth, gradually died of grief. The rulers who followed Muhammad Shah III were incapable and mired in disputes. The last ruler of the Bahamani kingdom was **Kareemulla (Kalimulla)**, who reigned only in name for three years and died in **1527**, at which point the Bahamani kingdom came to an end.

With the fall of the Bahamani kingdom, its regional governors became independent, giving rise to five successor kingdoms: the **Barid Shahi** at Bidar, the **Qutub Shahi** at Golconda, the **Adil Shahi** at Bijapur, the **Nizam Shahi** at Ahmadnagar, and the **Imad Shahi** at Berar.

### The Bahamani–Vijayanagara Wars

Warfare with Vijayanagara was, effectively, a standing duty of the Bahamani kings across the dynasty's history. These wars arose largely from long-standing economic and political causes, though both sides invoked religion to rouse their soldiers. Despite committing their full strength, the Bahamani sultans could never conquer Vijayanagara; the Vijayanagara kings repelled every invasion the Bahamani sultans led against them, preserving their self-respect and independence throughout.

The chief sources for reconstructing Bahamani rule fall into three broad categories: literary works, contemporary foreign accounts, and monuments.

**Persian and Sanskrit literary works**

*   **Fatwat-ut-Salatin**, written by Isami
*   **Bahaman Namah**, written by Adam
*   **Ishkanama** and **Hazairule Khuddus**, written by Gesudaraj
*   **Tariq-I-Faristha**, written by Faristha — explains the socio-religious and cultural conditions of the period
*   **Burhan-i-Masir**, written by Tabtaba — another chief source of Bahamani history

**Contemporary foreign accounts**

*   Writings of Niketin, Barbarossa, and Domingo Peas
*   Iban Batuta's travelogue **Rehalla**, which gives details of Bahamani rule
*   Letters and writings of Prime Minister Mohammad Gavan, which are also a main source

**Monuments and heritage**

*   Jami Masjid and Gesudaraj Darga at Gulbarga
*   Bidar fort and mosque
*   Rangin Mahal and Turkish Mahal at Bidar
*   The entrance gateways (darwazas) of these forts

### Concept of Kingship

In the medieval period, across India, Europe, and Asia, the king was the government and possessed divine rights. According to Amir Khusru, the Khalifa was considered the head of both the worldly and the divine world. In Persia, the Sassanid rulers built their court buildings like temples, and their subjects regarded the ruler as God and themselves as his slaves. Under pressure from the Ravindiya branch, some wanted the Khalifa to declare himself God, but the Khalifa resisted this and instead declared himself the divine ambassador (**Niyabutu-l-Khudavandi**). In this spirit, Udbi wrote that the emperor or Khalifa is God's shadow on earth (**Sultan Zill Allah-Fil-Arj**).

The Delhi Sultanate, established in A.D. 1206, carried this theory forward — rulers such as Mubarak Shah, Iltutmish, and Balban declared themselves divine slaves, divine shadows, and "the blessed one" (**Manjur-i-Rabbani**). Many later sultans, including the Deccan rulers and especially the Bahamani rulers, followed this same tradition of ruling as divine slaves.

### The Sultan's Authority

Allauddin Hassan Bahaman Shah, founder of the kingdom, ruled from Gulbarga and established a strong administrative system built on the principle that the word of the king is the law. All authority lay in him: he was head of the army, held the highest seat of Judiciary, and also acted as Chief Justice of the kingdom.

**Administrative divisions**

*   For administrative convenience the kingdom was divided into **Tarafs** (provinces), placed under the control of Amirs.
*   **Jagirs** were created within the kingdom, developing along lines similar to the feudal system.
*   The first Prime Minister of the Bahamani kingdom, holding the title **Vakil-i-Sultanate**, was **Malik Saifuddin Ghori**. Under his administration the kingdom extended from Gulbarga (the capital) to Daulatabad in the west, and in the south up to Raichur and Mudgal.
*   Chaul lay between the coastal area and Daulatabad. Bheed and Paithan were under the control of Mohammad Khan. In the north, Mahor, Ramgir, and parts of Berar were under the control of Sisthani. Bidar, Kaulas, and the Telangana districts were under the control of Azam Humayun.

### Seven Units of Administration (under Allauddin Hassan, per Burhan-i-Masir by Tabtaba)

| Officer | Function |
|---|---|
| Sahib-e-Arj | Army supervisor |
| Khurbegi Mesarsh | Left wing commander |
| Khurbegi Maimanath | Right wing commander |
| Dabir | Secretary |
| Diwan | Finance Minister |
| Sayyad-Ul-Khasba | In charge of divine affairs |
| Hajib-Ul-Khasba | Commissioner of the City |

### The Seven-Member Advisory Council

Hassan's successors modified the administrative system to suit changing needs, and an advisory council of seven officers was established to give advice and aid to the Sultan.

| Officer | Function |
|---|---|
| Vakil-us-Sultanate | Prime Minister — head of the council |
| Amir-I-Jumla | Finance Minister |
| Vazir-i-Ahsraf | Foreign Affairs Minister |
| Nazir | Finance Secretary |
| Kotwal | Police Officer |
| Vazir-I-Kul | Auditor |
| Sadar Jahan | Member of the Judiciary |

The head of the council was the Vakil-us-Sultanate, who had one secretary. Whenever the Sultan was out of the state, the Vakil acted as Vice-Sultan or Naib-Badshah. Amir Jumla looked after revenue collection — land tax, irrigation tax, forest tax, import and export duties, and other income — and reported to the King on income and expenditure. Vazir-I-Ashraf looked after foreign affairs, sent ambassadors to various countries, and discussed socio-religious and cultural affairs with the Sultan. 

The finance secretary maintained records of income, expenditure, taxes, and duties, and reported to Amir-I-Jumla on new taxes to be introduced, including on newly cultivated lands. Kotwal discharged police duties, maintained peace, law, and order, sometimes acted as a special judge, and supervised the jails. Sadar Jahan (also called Khaji-Ul-Khajat) was a member of the Judiciary who inquired into cases and ensured criminals were punished, and also looked after religious affairs.

The Sultan took special care in appointing ministers, discussing candidates personally and selecting efficient, honest, and highly talented persons. Royal family members were not appointed as ministers.

### The Royal Court and Durbar

All government affairs were conducted in the royal court, attended by ministers, officers of various departments, lords, and Ulemas. General issues were discussed in the Durbar and decisions taken there; the Durbar also received complaints from regional governments and provided solutions. The kings' orders and acts were read out in the durbar.

*   Mohammad Shah I enhanced the value of the Durbar by giving a place to the **Takt-I-Feroz** (throne).
*   The durbar was decorated with rare carpets and different colored curtains, and was filled with many bodyguards.
*   The durbar began every Friday morning and concluded before noon.
*   From the period of Mohammad Shah I, the honour of the durbar increased further — the Sultan received advice and instructions, and resolved controversies and treacheries through deep discussion with all present before taking a decision.

### Royal Palace Administration

During the "Bahaman Shah" period, administrative reforms relating to the Royal Palace were introduced, modelled on the Delhi Sultanate's system. According to Isami, the following jobs were created for the Royal Palace:

| Officer | Function |
|---|---|
| Vakil-I-Daar | Chief Supervisor of the Royal Palace |
| Barbuk | Teacher of the court festivals |
| Hajib | Welcomed and introduced guests; read the King's messages in court |
| Sa-Jandaz | Leader of the personal bodyguards of the Palace |
| Sarfdadar | Special bodyguard in the Royal Palace |
| Khurbak | Supervisor of Royal weaponry |
| Shahnai-I-Barag | Superintendent of the Court (Durbar) |
| Akurbuk | Supervisor of the Royal Horses |
| Shahna-I-Phil | Supervisor of the Elephants |
| Shahna-I-Khavan | Supervisor of the Royal Kitchen |
| Sarabdar | Supervisor of water supply |
| Khertadar | Additional officer of the troops |
| Sar-Dawat-dar | Additional officer of the Royal Stationery |
| Chesnigir | Officer who tasted the royal food |

Iban Batuta wrote in detail about many jobs within the Bahamani administration, and Isami similarly described many posts and the methods of recruitment used during the Bahamani period.

### Provincial Administration — Tarafs, Sarkars, and Paraganas

Bahamani rulers divided their kingdom into four regional states known as **Tarafs**; the officer of a Taraf was called a **Tarafdar**. The four Tarafs of the Allauddin Hassan period were:

| Taraf | Area Covered |
|---|---|
| Ahasanabad | Right side of Gulbarga to Dabhol, including the Tungabhadra and Krishna region |
| Daulatabad | Included Junnar and Paithan |
| Berar | Covered Mahor |
| Bidar | Covered Kandar, Induru, Kaulas, and other occupied areas of Telangana |

These provinces were also known as **Atrafs**, and their ruler was the Tarafdar, under whom many forts were maintained. The Tarafdar looked after peace, law, and order in his area, was personally appointed by the Sultan, and on the Sultan's advice appointed his own assistants. Civil and military affairs were looked after by the **Sar-I-Lashkar**.

Allauddin Hassan gave various titles to the Tarafdars: the Daulatabad Tarafdar received the title of **Masdi Ali**, the Berar Tarafdar received **Majlis Ali**, the Telangana Tarafdar received **Azam Humayun**, and the Gulbarga Tarafdar received **Vakil-Us-Sultanate**. Under the Tarafdars there were many **Thanedars**.

Administrative hierarchy below the Taraf, in descending order:

1.  **Taraf** (province) — under a Tarafdar
2.  **Sarkar** (like a modern district) — Tarafs were sub-divided into Sarkars
3.  **Paragana** (Tahasil) — Sarkars were further sub-divided into Paraganas
4.  **Village** — Paraganas were divided into villages, the most important and key unit of administration

Forts were under the control of an officer known as **Thanedar**, responsible for maintaining peace, law, and order in the fort's area.

Mohammad Gavan was the greatest Prime Minister among all the Prime Ministers of the Bahamani kingdom — indeed, among the most administratively capable Prime Ministers in the whole of Indian history. His father and grandfather had served as Vazirs under the ruler of Gilan in Iran. 

He belonged to the Gavan region, near "Refta" in northern Iran, and reached Mustafabad-Dhabol in **A.D. 1453**, coming to the Deccan from Iran at the age of 45. He first came to India as a trader, met Shah Muhibulla (grandson of Shah Niyamutulla Kirmani), and met the Bahamani Sultan Ahammad II before settling in Bidar, from where he rose to a higher position.

He was first appointed a **Mansabdar of 1000 soldiers**, and the second Muhammad Shah honoured him further with the title of **Amir**. During Humayun Shah's reign he earned the title **Malik-ul-Tujjar**. In **A.D. 1466**, at the request of his mother Muqduma-I-Jahan, Muhammad Shah III appointed Gavan as Prime Minister — from that day, effective administrative power passed into Gavan's hands even though the nominal rulers continued to hold the throne. Despite wielding this power, Gavan remained loyal throughout his life and served the state faithfully.

### Curbing the Power of the Foreign Amirs

During the Bahamani sultans' time, foreign Amirs had grown extremely powerful — for instance, **Malik Tuchar**, an Amir belonging to a Caucasus/Anatolian community, commanded two lakh soldiers, and there were other Amirs like him. Such Amirs, if they chose, were strong enough to depose a king. 

As Prime Minister, Gavan reduced the strength of the Amirs who posed a danger to the kingdom, brought the armies under their control into direct state control, and reorganised them into divisions, taking firm measures to train the soldiers systematically. Through this, he turned the army into a formidable, near-invincible force.

### Administrative Appointments and Reforms

**Appointments made by Gavan**

*   Yusuf Adil — appointed Sar-Lashkar of Daulatabad
*   Malika Hassan — appointed Sar Lashkar of Telangana
*   Fatullah — appointed Sar Lashkar of Berar
*   Dariyakhan, Khasimbeg, and Shah Quli — appointed as his personal servants

**Reforms introduced by Gavan**

*   Introduced exact land tax assessment, classification of lands, and evaluation of soil fertility and crop yields
*   Surveyed the lands of the kingdom
*   Took strict measures to root out bribery and corruption
*   Successfully reformed both the legal and military spheres
*   Established many schools in Bidar city and built one of the biggest Madarsas there, to promote education
*   Captured the forts of **Rajamahendravaram (Rajamundry) and Kondavidu**

In **1475**, a terrible famine struck the Deccan. Taking advantage of this, the king of Orissa attacked Telangana; Muhammad Shah repelled the attack, and wrote to the Orissa kings declaring that they had no rights whatsoever over Telangana. Muslim rule continued in Telangana without interruption for about **600 years**, from the Bahamani period down to the Nizam's time.

### Character and Personal Life

Gavan was an extraordinarily high-minded person who upheld many ideals. Despite holding great power in his hands, he never boasted of it. He slept on a simple leather mat and ate from earthen vessels. He performed many acts of charity, and established a great library in Bidar city, gathering together some three thousand rare manuscripts and books. Yet even such a virtuous and accomplished person could not escape the era's religious intolerance — Gavan, too, destroyed a number of temples that lay along the routes of his military campaigns.

Scholars such as Maulana Nooruddin Jami (a great Persian researcher), Sheik Sadruddin, and Abdur Rehaman Ravasi came to the Deccan and settled there, contributing greatly to its literature during this period.

### Sectarian Rivalry and Gavan's Murder

During the Bahamani kings' time, large numbers of people who came from Persia and settled in the Deccan came to be known as **Afaqis** (or Apaki chiefs); they belonged to the Shia sect, and the Sultans showed them particular favour, giving them high posts. 

Deccan-settled Sunnis, who traced their standing back to representing the Delhi Sultanate in the region, formed the majority of the faithful. Rivalry between the Shia and Sunni factions in the Bahamani kingdom grew intense. Gavan himself stayed away from this religious hostility, but the local Deccan Amirs resented his growing prominence and plotted against him.

Conspirators spread a rumour, in league with the Orissa kings, that Gavan was secretly writing letters to defame the Sultan. Believing this rumour, the Sultan — who had for so long guarded his kingdom as carefully as the eyelid guards the eye — had Mahmud Gavan murdered in **A.D. 1481**. With Gavan's murder, the very foundations of the Bahamani kingdom were shaken.

He earned a permanent name in Bahamani history as a great soldier, administrator, scholar, and legal exponent, and wrote two books — **Riyajul Insha** and **Manjirul Insha**.

Due to frequent wars with Vijayanagara and Malwa, and internal conflicts, the Bahamani rulers developed a very strong military system, organised into two types:

1.  **Central military system**
2.  **Regional military system**

### Central Military System

The head of the central military system was the **Amir-Ul-Umra**, the highest official next to the Sultan. He commanded a contingent of 1,500 soldiers; below him, officials held contingents of 1,000, 500, 300, and 100 soldiers.

For the maintenance of the army, the Sultan provided land grants or fixed income:

*   An officer maintaining 500 soldiers was given one lakh, or **Iqta (Jagir)** land.
*   An officer maintaining 1,000 soldiers was given two lakh, or land equal to that income, as Iqta (Jagir) land.

During Allauddin Hassan's period, the central government army had **50,000 horse riders** and **25,000 infantry**. Later, during Muhammad Shah's period and after, the central army strength increased to **one lakh and nine thousand**. Along with this growth in numbers came changes in training and strategy.

### Regional Military System

In the regional army, the **Tarafdar** was the head, discharging both civil and military duties; in this military capacity he was called **Sar Lashkar**. Many forts existed under regional control, each typically with 1,000 soldiers (sometimes increasing to 10,000). Whenever the Sultan desired, the Tarafdar also discharged military duties directly.

### Composition and Equipment

The Bahamani army included both Hindu and Muslim soldiers, and was organised into many **Lashkars**. Every Lashkar included elephants and guns. Important weapons of the time were maces, axes, swords, arrows, and guns.

Faristha recorded that the Bahamanis used guns; the place where guns were stored was called **Atish Khana**, headed by an officer called **Mir-i-Atish**. According to Faristha, Mahammad Shah defeated the Vijayanagara king due to the use of guns. Barbosa gave a detailed account of Muhammad Shah's wars during A.D. 1482–1518, describing the strategies, attacks, army contingents, and weapons used.

Overall, the Bahamani rulers relied on fast-moving cavalry and modern weaponry with large army contingents. Tents and war camps were set up near the battlefield, and soldiers took their wives with them to the battlefield. The secret of their victories in war lay largely in their horse troops.

The highest office of the Judiciary was the Sultan himself, whose seat was the Supreme Court. The Bahamanis belonged to the Sunni sect; the Imad Shahis (Berar) and the Barid Shahi (Bidar) were also Sunni Muslims, while the Bijapur, Ahemadnagar, and Golconda rulers were Shias.

**Principles of the legal system**

*   All rulers executed the legal system as per the Shariat — the order of the Bahamani Sultan was the law.
*   Under Islamic legal tradition, people were expected first to worship Prophet Mohammad, and then to respect and obey the Sultan.
*   Drinking alcohol in open places was prohibited.
*   Immorality and corruption were prohibited.
*   Employees were severely punished for neglecting their duties.

**Instances of punishment**

*   During the period of Allauddin Ahamad Shah II, his secretary (Sarmad-i-Kar-i-mulki) Mustahfa Khan Sayyad sent letters without the Sultan's prior permission; he was punished by beheading and his body was exhibited on the main road.
*   Allauddin Ahmad Shah II punished the grandson of Hazrat Sayyad Gesudaraj for drinking alcohol — he was publicly beaten 200 times and made to take an oath never to drink again.
*   Anyone who rebelled against the king was severely punished, sometimes by beheading; rebellion for the throne invited especially strong punishment, sometimes by plucking out the offender's eyes. Officers who failed to suppress rebellion were also punished severely.
    *   Saif Khan, who opposed Humayun Shah Bahamani's accession, was punished by being tied to an elephant's legs and paraded through the town.
    *   Prince Hassan Khan, who rebelled against the Sultan, was punished by having his eyes plucked out and was imprisoned.
*   During the period of Mohammad Shah I Bahamani, an effort was made to eliminate theft: within six months, 20,000 thieves were severely punished and theft was brought under control.

### Judicial Hierarchy

*   **Sadar-I-Sharia** — head of the judicial system next to the Sultan, supervised judicial enquiry and the severity of punishment for crimes, and worked to create a crime-free kingdom.
*   In the **Tarafs** (provincial states), the head of Judiciary was the **Sadar**, who enquired into and punished crimes occurring in the provinces. Promiscuity was prohibited, though in practice this could not always be stopped, along with looting, thefts, violence, illegal activities, and rebellions.
*   In the cities, the **Khaji** was the Judge; in big cities, a **Naib-Khaji** was also appointed to assist the Khaji.
*   One **Mufti** was appointed to every court, to explain legal matters and preserve judgments in writing.
*   To every city and fort, one **Kotwal** was appointed, who maintained peace and law and order, brought criminals to the courts, and held other protective responsibilities.
*   **Mahatashibs** were appointed to check whether people were genuinely following the Shariat, and to create religious awareness among the people.
*   To solve the problems of soldiers, an advocate called **Khaji Asker** was appointed. During Allauddin Hassan Bahamani's period, one Munajim Badakshi held this post — soldiers who committed crimes, neglected duty, or leaked secret information to enemies were investigated and punished under this office.
*   In the **Paragana**, the judge was the **Khaji**, assisted by the **Havaldar** and a **Majlis** (which handled only civil cases). The head of the paragana was the Havaldar, also known as **Maksadar**.
*   After the conquest of Warangal, Ahemad Shah established **Thanas**, headed by a **Thanedar**, who looked after law and order in his area, assisted by the Kotwal.
*   In the villages, **Mukhaddam** and **Gotas** conducted the administration, resolving disputes, holding judicial enquiries, and punishing criminals.

Selection of judges was done cautiously: they were required to be highly moral and ethical, well-versed in customs and traditions, thorough practitioners of religious rituals, educationally accomplished scholars, and experts in both Hindu and Islamic principles. Only such meritorious persons were appointed as Judges.

Bahamani sultans and their successors established a permanent police system for maintaining peace and law and order. In the capital city, every city in the kingdom, and every fort, a police officer called **Kotwal** was appointed, who acted as both police commissioner and municipal commissioner in the city; the Kotwal of a fort also acted as a military officer there. In the cities, an officer called **Samaubatan** was appointed to assist the Kotwal.

*   **Siladar**: an office first appointed by Muhammad Shah Bahamani (following the practice of the Delhi Sultans), responsible for protecting the kingdom, organising guards, and appointing guards to carry weapons from place to place.
*   **Samaubat**: an officer belonging to the upper strata, who commanded four thousand bodyguards. For protection of the Royal palace, five Siladars and one thousand bodyguards were appointed, on duty the whole day. Only a person fully trustworthy to the Sultan was appointed as Samaubat.

Kotwal was directly answerable to the Sultan and was the key person controlling crime in his jurisdiction. He was in charge of jails and jailors; his responsibilities included enquiring into and producing the accused before judges, and — once charges were proved — taking the person into custody and implementing the court's punishment. In big cities, the Kotwal was assisted by assistants called **Naib-Kotwal**. Police administration acted severely to control crime in the cities, forts, and other important places of the kingdom.

After the establishment of the Bahamani kingdom in the Deccan, the influence of the upper-class Hindu society gradually decreased, including in administration, since the Bahamani kingdom was a Muslim state — in the king's court and Durbar, the role of upper-class Hindus became negligible, and the ministers were mostly Muslims. 

This was encouraged especially under the Tughluq rule in Delhi and continued particularly during the Allauddin Hassan period. Families such as the Gorpajis, Nimbalkars of Paithan, Manes of Masvad, and Godjes of Malawadi could exert some influence on administration but could not obtain ministerial posts; they instead became army officers in the Jagirs due to their close relations with Hassan.

**Dakhanis and Garibhus**: the upper-class people of the time were divided into two groups — the **Dakhanis** (local/old settlers) and the **Garibhus** (newcomers). There was strong confrontation and competition between the two for status and authority, though the powerful Sultans kept this in check. 

Prime Minister Mohammad Gavan managed to control this rivalry, but afterward the conflict could not be contained, and this local-versus-non-local issue eventually contributed to the downfall of the kingdom. This local–newcomer rivalry ran alongside a religious dimension as well: newcomers from Persia, known as **Afaqis**, mostly followed the Shia sect and were favoured with high posts by the Sultans, while the older, Deccan-settled community was predominantly Sunni — and rivalry between the two sects grew intense in the kingdom's later years.

Although the Bahamani rulers and higher officials were Muslims, the majority of the population remained Hindu; social formation in the Deccan was similar to that of North India, and caste divisions were based on occupation and profession.

### Social Classes

Similar to North India, Deccan society in the 14th century was divided into four classes: **Brahmins** (upper class), followed by **Kshatriyas**, **Vaisyas**, and **Sudras**. After the Kshatriya class, the **Kayasthas** held an important position in society at that time.

In the Hindu kingdom of Vijayanagara, Brahmins, traders, handicraft workers, weavers, and barbers occupied the social hierarchy, while the **Dombaras (Dommera, or soothsayers)**, **Jogis**, and **Marwars** were considered low-class people.

*   Upper-class Brahmins served as ministers, army generals, army chiefs, and religious advisers, occupying an important position in society.
*   Kshatriyas looked after administrative affairs.
*   Other services were provided by traders and Vaisyas.
*   Sudras provided all types of services.

### Marriage System

Brahmins married within the same caste but not within the same **Gotra** — marriage within the same Gotra was prohibited among Brahmins. Marriage with a niece (sister's daughter) was in vogue among Lingayats. Among Reddy, Lingayat, and other caste communities, marriage within the same caste and same Gotra was common practice.

**Divorce**: divorce was very difficult in this period, but was permitted if the husband was handicapped, a leper, of unfit mental state, unfit for sexual acts, or suffering from an incurable disease — in such cases the wife was eligible for divorce. Similarly, if the wife was barren, did not cooperate with the husband in sexual acts, or failed to bear a male child, the husband could divorce her and remarry.

**Widow remarriage and Sati**: widow remarriage was against the rules of the period. According to the **Brihaspati Smriti**, a wife was expected to die immediately after her husband's death — this practice was called **Sati** — and it was followed by the upper classes. When the Bahamanis defeated the Reddy kings, queens of the defeated Reddy kings performed Sati, as recorded by Faristha. Sati was not practiced among the Sudras. Iban Batuta, Nicole Conti, and Barbosa all recorded that Sati was prohibited in the Deccan for pregnant women, women carrying children, and Sudra women.

The book **Guru Charitra** greatly praised the practice of Sati; Yadava Ramadeva's queen Kamaisa is recorded as having become Sati. Lower castes and classes did not follow Sati and instead practiced widow remarriage; among upper castes and classes, widow remarriage was prohibited. Women of the lower classes and castes had greater freedom and equal participation in fairs and festivals.

**Dowry**: dowry was compulsory at the time of marriage. There existed a concept called **"Sthree Dhan"**, which was in vogue among the upper classes and common across the Deccan. If Sthree Dhan was not given as part of the dowry, the husband was required to give the wife an equal share in his property on par with his sons.

### Family Life

The joint family system was common, with the eldest member looking after household affairs; even when brothers lived separately, they participated together in religious performances, festivals, and fairs. Polygamy and polyandry had religious acceptance among Muslims but were not practiced much in reality. Faristha recorded that child marriage was common in this period, and works such as **Jnaneshwari** and **Leela Charitra** support the existence of child marriages.

Brahmins rode on horseback during marriage ceremonies; contemporary writings show that Dehsmukhs, Kumbhi, Sutar, Lohar, Gurav, Sonar, Daangar, Jangam, Mahar, and Bheel communities also used horses in marriage processions, and horses were used in Muslim marriages too. 

The Mang community's bride rode on a buffalo, while the Kaikaris and Burudus did not use any animal — the bride simply walked. Other communities, especially artisans, rode a bull for the procession; Teli, Chamar, Navi, Kumbhar, and Gopal communities used the bull during the bride's marriage procession. Marriage ceremonies were celebrated over many days.

Women of the upper class followed the Sati practice, with an exception made for women with children and pregnant women. Yadava Ramadeva's queen Kamaisa became Sati, and the book **Guru Charitra** greatly praised the Sati practice. People of the lower castes and classes did not follow Sati and instead practiced widow remarriage; for upper castes and classes, widow remarriage was prohibited. Women of the lower classes and castes enjoyed more freedom and equal participation in fairs and festivals.

### Houses

The Sultan lived in the Royal Palace, which was surrounded by a variety of fruit gardens and was situated at the centre. The Sultan, ministers, officers, and royal family members lived in large, highly decorated palaces filled with different types of household items, furniture, chairs, and curtains. Niketan recorded that the lords led a lavish life, reflecting their social status.

Houses were built on strong foundations, with walls constructed of mud and foundations laid with hard stones — this was confirmed by excavations at Navesa (Ahemadnagar district of Maharashtra). A typical house consisted of three or four rooms, one of which was a kitchen; the upper ceiling was made of mud and grass. Use of mud in house construction was common across all house types in this period. Rich people's houses typically had one verandah, a drawing room, and four rooms. Excavations at Nevasa uncovered glasses, big jars, bathing tubs, big globes, big plates, and cutlery items commonly used at the time.

### Food

Different varieties of rice were used, with good-quality rice consumed by the higher classes, generally eaten with curd, buttermilk, and various leafy vegetables. On medical advice, patients ate limited food — less sugar, rice, and milk. Wheat, millets (jawar), and barley were also eaten; green gram was used in food, and bread made from jawar powder was the staple menu of the common people. 

Wheat bread mixed with ghee and milk was taken by the high classes; sunflower oil was widely consumed. On special occasions, sugar and jaggery were also consumed, along with different types of pickles. Laddu, pancake, khaddu, and kheer (prepared with milk) were also part of the diet.

Niketan recorded that Hindus of different faiths did not dine together, reflecting the caste system of the period. Some communities ate meat, pigeons, fish, and eggs; Hindu kings mostly belonged to the Maratha or Reddy communities. Higher-class ladies remained behind the veil, or "Pardha." Niketan noted that in Brahmin localities, people did not eat meat, pigeons, fish, or pork, suggesting Brahmins largely resided in such areas. 

Lingayats and some other castes did not take non-vegetarian food, and Brahmins ate only twice a day; ghee and milk formed part of their diet. Common people ate a variety of foods. According to Isami, both vegetarian and non-vegetarian food was prepared in the Sultan's palace, betel leaves were chewed after meals, and imported Chinese tableware was used for dining in the palace.

### Dress

People generally wore the **Dhoti** and **Uttariam**, along with a tied head-dress. Scholars and poets frequently wore two-piece clothes, and wearing footwear was common. Ladies wore sarees and cholis (blouses). During fairs and festivals, silk and costly dress was worn by people of the higher class. 

Woolen blankets were used in winter, similar to those used by Muslims in Delhi. Two-piece cloths were used as head-dress; silk dress was worn beyond the elbow, and another dress beyond the knee was used, along with trousers, petticoats, and dupattas that covered the body fully. Both Hindus and Muslims wore different ornaments, including neck ornaments and rings studded with colored stones. During summer, the Uttariam was not worn by common people, and farmers and craftsmen never wore the Uttariam.

During the Bahamani period, society was divided into three economic classes:

1.  **Upper class** — high officers, Iqtadars, Ulemas, and court employees, who received sufficient income from the government, led a lavish life, and kept servants and soldiers.
2.  **Middle class** — religious heads, Brahmins, Muslims, small land lords, Tarafdars, local traders, and other employees; they possessed some horses, some servants, and owned houses, acquiring their daily needs without obstruction and leading a somewhat lavish life. Barbosa described that at Calicut, traders possessed servants and horses, dressed well, and led a happy life — a similar happy life was led by traders of the Deccan. In trade and commerce, some individuals rose to high status: Malik-Ul-Tujjar, for example, was appointed Prime Minister.
3.  **Lower class** — farmers, craftsmen, and daily wagers, who, as recorded by Moreland, led a difficult life. Farmers in particular faced hardship due to low rainfall, small land holdings, and indebtedness. According to Niketan, "professionals and daily wagers" fared better in life than farmers, who faced many difficulties.

Bahamani rulers and Amirs encouraged professional workers, and different types of cottage industries were promoted, with their production exported to foreign countries. **Bidar, Gulbarga, Warangal, Raichur, Nanded, and Bhuvanagiri** became famous for cottage industries, providing employment and benefit to artisans.

### Revenue System

Agriculture was the main occupation of the people, depending mostly on rainfall, though artificial tanks and canals also provided irrigation. Crop land was divided into three types:

1.  **Metta** (dry) land
2.  **Magani** (wet) land
3.  **Gaddi** (grass) land

One-sixth of the produce was collected as land tax. During the rule of Mohammad Shah, a land survey was conducted under the supervision of Gavan, and land tax was decided based on fertility and irrigation facility available. Wet lands, cash crops, and gardens were taxed more heavily, while dry lands attracted less tax. Land under active cultivation was taxed, while fallow land was given tax exemption. Land donated to temples and mosques was exempted from land tax, and some land was granted for providing services in the villages.

### Trade and Commerce

The Bahamanis maintained commercial relations with Persia, Africa, Europe, and other western countries. Exports mainly took place from the ports of **Goa, Dabhol, Mahim, and Machilipatnam**. Niketan recorded that these were first-grade ports, and Dabhol was a particularly important port. Faristha noted that many ships were used for commercial purposes, and textiles, Bidri wares, and Warangal carpets were among the goods exported from these ports.

**Imports** included gold, spices, China porcelain and scent items, drugs, high-quality horses, pearls, and slaves. According to Barbosa, sugar was exported in large quantities to Sri Lanka, Arabia, and Persia.

### Taxes

Bahamanis collected many taxes through a dedicated tax-collecting department. A contemporary work, **Mahaboob-Ul-Vatan**, records the different taxes imposed on various items during Bahamani rule:

| Item | Tax |
|---|---|
| Horses | One Dinar |
| Cow and buffalo | One Phanam |
| Goat | Five Jital |
| Camel | Half Jelool |
| Elephant | One Dinar |

In addition, import duty was collected on silk and cotton textiles (three rupees and eight annas per hundred rupees) and on gold and silver ornaments (seven rupees and eight annas per hundred rupees). Salt tax was also collected. There was no tax on wood and grass.

### Coins

Currency was minted at the Gulbarga and Bidar mints, with some Bahamani coins also minted at Fatehbad. Bahamani coins were made of gold, silver, and copper. During the period of Allauddin Bahaman Shah, coins existed in three types of measurements; during Muhammad Shah I's period, coins of a single measurement were used. Big-measurement coins were introduced by Muhammad Shah II. The Sultans paid close attention to coin-making and the functioning of the mints, and circulation of fake coins was strictly prohibited.

Bahamani rulers actively encouraged industries and handicrafts, and their production was exported to foreign countries.

*   **Cotton and silk mills** were established in many places.
*   **Iron and steel works** were carried out at Paithan.
*   **Silk clothes** were manufactured at Daulatabad, Gulbarga, and Khidki, and were available at cheaper rates; these were exported and also supplied to local Amirs.
*   **Mashur, Heemru, Sarees, Dhotis, Dorias, and Mulmal cloths** were manufactured across different regions.
*   Amirs purchased **"Pagadis"** (a type of head-dress), manufactured at Raichur and Nanded.
*   **Bidar** was popular for pot-making — the **Bidri** craft became popular not only within India but also internationally, and continues to be practiced in many places today.
*   **Warangal** became famous for **carpet making**. Percy Brown recorded that very large beams were manufactured in the Deccan, made of iron.
*   **War equipment** — swords, water cans, bows, knives, and arrows — was also manufactured in the Deccan. **Nalgonda, Bhuvanagiri, and Adilabad, Nirmal** were popular centres for these.
*   **Copper** was mined at Chota Nagapur in the Deccan and exported to various places; Marco Polo also discussed this. Niketan recorded Raichur's diamonds.
*   **Leather industry** was an important industry of the Bahamani kingdom, especially goat leather; leather was exported to Arabia and Persia from the **Thana port**.
*   **Ship building**: Allauddin Bahaman II possessed boats bigger than those of the Italians. Contemporary literary works mention shipbuilding during this period, and the Bahamani Shahs used small ships; crossing the Tungabhadra river, the Bahamanis attacked the Vijayanagara kings twice. The Bahamanis made great progress in shipbuilding overall — their ships were noted as more durable and larger in build than those of Italy.
*   **Bijapur** was very famous for its **textile industry**; textiles were exported to Persia, Arabia, and East Africa, with **Calico and Muslin** being important cloth varieties. Barbosa recorded that Portuguese traders purchased and exported these daily.
*   **Velvet, Scarlet, Satin, and Damakas**, and woolen clothes, were imported **from Goa**.

Many of these industries were encouraged by the Bahamani rulers, Amirs, Jagirdars, and Izaradars.

### Hindu Reform Movements Before the Bahamani Period

Prior to the establishment of Bahamani rule, a social reform movement had already begun in South India. In the seventh century, the Pallavas and Chalukyas patronized Hinduism, and as a result Buddhism and Jainism weakened while Saivism and Vaisnavism gained ground; Hinduism thereby re-established itself.

Due to the wider Bhakti movement, Saivism rose to new heights under the leadership of **Tirugnana Sambandhar, Tirunavakkarasu, Sundara Murthy, and Manikavashar**; the **Alvars** — including Andal, Kulashekar, Tirumangai, and Nammalvar, some of whom belonged to low castes — inspired the Vaisnava philosophy. These two movements taught equality before God, idol worship, suppression of unwanted desires, divine devotion, and love towards animals.

**Shankaracharya** led the Bhakti movement on the Advaita side; along with **Nadamuni, Ramanuja, and Nimbarka**, he was a key figure of this movement, aimed at the renaissance of Hinduism and the weakening of Buddhism and Jainism through new methods of religious practice.

At the same time, a religious reform movement was underway in Karnataka: the **Lingayat movement**, founded by **Basava and Chenna Basava** in the twelfth century. This movement spread further during Bahamani rule and taught the ideals of brotherhood, criticizing the caste system.

### Hindu Pilgrimage Centres

Nasik and Paithan were pious centres for Hindus; many people took a dip in the River Godavari for the absolving of sins. The Vithoba temple at Pandaripur was a pious place for both Kannadigas and Marathis. Dattatreya was the chief deity at the pious place of Ganagapur. 

The Bhavani Temple at Tulzapur was famous — according to an inscription of A.D. 1398, a fair was held there every year, started during the Feroz Shah period. Tulzapur, Kolhapur, Matapur, and Saptashrungi were the four important Bhavani places. Sirpur, near Akola, was a Jaina worshipping place, and Riddipur, near Buldana, was famous for the **Mahanubhavas**.

### Islam and Sufism

Alongside Hinduism, Islam — established by Prophet Mohammad — played a very important role in Bahamani society. During this period, Muslims were divided into four classes: (1) lords of the army and civil officers, (2) traders, (3) slaves, and (4) poets, scholars, and religious heads. 

Slavery was common in Islamic society, and slaves were sometimes raised to the level of Sultan under Bahamani patronage — among the slaves, **Yusuf, Adil Khan, Malik Hassan, and Khasim Barida** rose to high status. Ulemas, Khajis, Amirs, Muftis, Khatibus, and Imams occupied important administrative positions and were patronized by the state.

For the strengthening of Islam, the **Sufi movement** developed in the Deccan.

*   **Khaja Bande Nawaz Gesudaraj** (of Gulbarga) was the chief exponent of Sufism in the Deccan; his durbar was visited by both Hindus and Muslims. Born in Delhi in **A.D. 1321**, he reached Gulbarga at the age of 90, in **1402–03**; his father, Syed Yousuf, had come to Daulatabad during Mohammad Bin Tughluq's period.

*   Gesudaraj lived in the Deccan from 1324 to 1331, constructed a **KhanKa** at Gulbarga for his followers and disciples, and preached the **Chisti order** of Sufism. He died in **1422**. Even today, people from Telangana, Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Andhra attend the **Urs** festivals held in his memory.

*   **Burhanuddin** explained the Chisti principles at Daulatabad.
*   The Sufi orders active in the Deccan included **Chisti, Suhravardhi, Sattari, and Khadri**.
*   **Shiek Ainuddin** of Bijapur and **Shiek Shirajuddin Junaidi** were important Sufis during Allauddin Hassan Bahaman Shah's period.
*   **Shah Niyamatulla Khadri** settled in the Deccan, preaching and expanding the Khadri branch of Sufism, attracting many followers through his teaching and made Islam a stable religion in the Deccan.

### Sufi Philosophy and Hindu–Muslim Syncretism

In the twelfth century, some of the Muhammadans who arrived in the Deccan from Persia and the Middle East were Sufis. They showed a spirit of brotherhood and thereby attracted Hindus toward them. Central to Sufi philosophy was cultivating true love (prema) for God — those who showed genuine love for God were held to draw close to God, and this was the essence of what Sufi teaching preached. 

Formal prayer, fasting, and vows were not, in the Sufis' own view, the most essential things. Because their teaching was rooted in love for God, Sufi philosophy did not carry hostility toward other faiths; Sufis held that all religions were different paths leading toward the same God, with the upliftment of humanity as their chief goal.

In the Deccan, Hindu–Muslim unity of this kind began during the reign of **Firoz Shah Bahamani**, and spread widely, taking deep root during the reign of his brother **Ahmad Shah**. Hindus of the time observed Ahmad Shah's Urs according to the Hindu calendar (Panchangam); they regarded him almost as a saint, worshipping him with devotion and offerings of flowers. The priest who conducted this Urs festival at Gulbarga was, notably, a **Lingayat Jangam**.

During the rule of the Deccan sultans, the **Pandharipur tradition** rose to prominence. Being a monotheistic (Ekeshwaravada) tradition, it mixed with unorthodox local practices and, in doing so, helped this tradition take hold. The founder of this tradition was the great devotee **Jnaneshwar**, whose teachings created a new spiritual consciousness and vitality; he taught that a person is not made great by caste, and that in God's eyes all people are equal.

In Kurnool district, at **Srisailam**, the **Nada** tradition flourished, with Yogis who were its prophets spreading its teaching widely. By the 15th century, the **Dattatreya tradition** had become strong in the Deccan; among Dattatreya's devotees were a number of Muslims, who became well known as **Shahi Fakirs**.

The Bahamani sultans patronised the **Urdu language**, which in that period was known as **Hindavi**. No sustained effort to forcibly convert Hindus to Islam took place under Bahamani rule, in contrast to the practice under the Delhi Empire. Musunuri Kapaya Nayaka, who ruled well, had believed the emergence of an independent Bahamani kingdom would work in his favour, and hoped that the Gulbarga and Warangal kingdoms could coexist peacefully side by side — a hope that was dashed within a short time, after which the Warangal kingdom fell under Bahamani control.

Nasik and Paithan were the centres of Hindu scholarship. In **A.D. 1290**, the **Jnaneshwari** was compiled at Nevasa. Gangapur was the Vedic centre. Students commonly began their education with texts such as **Amarakosha, Roopavali, Samaschakra, Panchatantra, and Hitopadesha**. **Trivikram Bharati of Kumashi** was a great Vedic researcher of the 14th century. Students received education by going to their teachers directly.

**Islamic education** flourished at Gulbarga, Bidar, Kandahar, Elichpur, Daulatabad, Junnar, Chaut, and Dhabol, which continued as Islamic centres. Recitation of the **Quran** was carried out in an elaborate way, and the reading of **Hadis** was also important. In **A.D. 1472**, **Mohammad Gavan built a great college at Bidar**, which became the great centre of Islamic education in the Deccan; scholars such as **Jalaluddin Davvani and Sadruddin Ravvasi** visited this centre. 

Gavan also developed the Madarsa library extensively; **calligraphy** developed into a prominent art form, and education continued in Arabic and Persian. At **Elichpur**, the **Darul-Uloom** (educational school) was established, which collected 3000 Dinars in yearly fees; alongside religious education, literature was also taught in the Madarsas.

Teachers gave special attention to their students, and discipline and character were given great importance in society. The Bahamani rulers took special care for the development of education.

Many scholarly works were compiled during the Bahamani period, chiefly by leaders of the Bhakti and Sufi traditions, who enlightened society through their writing.

**Bhakti/Marathi and regional literature**

*   **Jnanadev**, a Maharashtra ascetic, wrote **Jnaneshwari**.
*   **Namadev** led the Bhagavata sect.
*   The **Mahanubhava sect** was established by **Chakradhar**, who wrote **Laila Charitra** in Marathi; this work was divided into Ekanka, Purvardha, and Uttarardha.
*   **Narendra and Parushurama** wrote a book called **Smriti Sthal**.
*   **Vishwanatha**, native of Balapur, wrote **Jnaan Probodh** in **1331**.
*   **Ravalo Bhasa** wrote **Guhyadri Varnana** in **A.D. 1333**.
*   **Narayanabasa** wrote **Raddipurva Varnana** in **1331**.
*   **Meru Swamy** wrote two great works, **Bheemopadesham** and **Ramasohalalu**.
*   **Vamana Pandita** wrote **Yadhartha Deepika**.
*   **Madhavcharya** compiled **Jaiminiya Nyayamala Vistari**.
*   **Ramanujacharya** wrote **Tantra Rahashya**.
*   **Vidyaranya** wrote **Panchadashi**, **Jeevanmukti Viveka**, and another work titled **Sarvadarshana Samgraha**.
*   **Dharmaraja dwari** wrote **Vedanta Paribhasha**.
*   **Madhava Saraswati** of Karnataka wrote **Sarvadarshana Kaumudi**.
*   **Sripati** wrote **Srikarabhashya**.
*   **Madhavacharya** preached the **Dvaita philosophy**; **Shankaracharya** preached **Advaita philosophy**.
*   **Jayateertha** wrote a commentary on **Nyayasudha**.
*   **Keshava Bhattu** wrote **Tarka Deepika**; **Varadaraju** wrote **Vevahara Nirnaya**; scholar **Mahadeva** wrote **Kamadhenu**.

**Persian literature and Sufi/court poets** Many books were also written in Persian during this period, by writers across Gulbarga, Raichur, Ahamadnagar, Aurangabad, Daulatabad, and Golconda.

*   **Isami** was the greatest writer of the Bahamani period, and wrote **Putawat Salaatin**; he was the first great poet under Bahamani rule.
*   **Khaja Bande Nawaz Gesudaraj**, besides being a great Sufi scholar and teacher, was also a great poet — he wrote **Anishul-Ushak**, compiled in Arabic and Persian. He also wrote **Mahirikul Anwar** (on the systems and traditions of Prophet Mohammad's period), commentaries on **Avaripool Mariff** (originally by Shiek Shihbuddin Suhra), **Taruf** (by Shiek Abubaker Mohammad bin Bukhari), and **Adabul Mureedin** (by Shiek Nazeebuddin Abdul Basheer Suhravardhi), as well as **Khaddoos, Ishka Nama, Asammarul Asrar,** and **Khatima**. He preached brotherhood, symbolic of religious harmony.
*   **Adhari** (full name Nooruddin Hanji) wrote many works, including **Javahirull Asra, Meerathul Asral (Matnavi)**, and **Si-I-Safa**; the poet **Deewan Adhari** died before completing the writing of **Bahaman Nama**, which was thereafter completed by **Nazeeri and Sami**.
*   **Nazeeri** earned great fame during the rule of Allauddin Ahamad; **Nazeeri Mulla**, along with Sami, completed the **Bahaman Nama**.
*   **Faristha** was born in **1552** at Astrabad, was later brought to Ahemadnagar, and subsequently joined the court of the second Ibrahim Adil Shah; he died in **1623** at Bijapur. He wrote **Gulshan-I-Ibrahimi**, also known as **Tariq-I-Faristha**, an important work analyzing the socio-economic and religious conditions of the period.
*   **Sirajat-Tawarik** was written by Mulla Mohammad Lari; **Tahufatoon-Salatin** was written by Mulla Dawood Bidri; Mulla Abdul Kareem Handani's **"Life of Mohammad Gavan"** also helps in understanding the contemporary conditions of the period.

Bahamani rulers undertook extensive construction across the Deccan, beginning first at Gulbarga, where they built mosques and tombs.

*   **Muhammad Shah** built a great mosque at Gulbarga in **A.D. 1367**, constructed under the supervision of Rafi-Bin-Shams-bin-Mansur Khajvini; it measured 216 feet from east to west and 176 feet from north to south.
*   **Gesudaraj's Darga** was constructed two years after his death, taking seven years to complete; it was built during the rule of Ahammada Vali, with a large dome.
*   During the period of **Ahammada Vali**, the capital was shifted from Gulbarga to **Bidar**.
*   During the **Feroz Shah** period, a new town, **Firozabad**, was constructed 12 miles from Gulbarga.
*   During Ahammada Vali's period, architects from **Turkey, Baghdad, Iran, Arabia, Rome, and North India** came to Bidar and contributed to its construction and design.
*   At **Bidar**, the following were constructed: the Bidar fort, the Royal Palace, the sixteen-pillared mosque (**Sola Khambha Masjid**), tombs, and Madarsas. Within the Bidar fort, the **Rangeen Mahal** was beautifully constructed. **Gagan Mahal, Tarkash Mahal, Cheeni Mahal, Nageen Mahal**, and the Royal bathrooms were built during the rule of Mohammad Shah Bahamani.
*   At **Ashtura** village, the tombs of Bahamani rulers were built; among them, the tomb of Ahammada Shah Vali is especially large.
*   The Madarsa built by Gavan became the most prominent one of its kind.
*   The construction of Bidar town was carried out under Ahamad Shah Vali.
*   **Rauz-I-Shiek** and the **Feroz Shah Tombs** were built as part of the **Hafta Gumbaz** complex. Many other tombs and mosques were constructed at various places across the kingdom.

Bahamani rule spanned roughly **A.D. 1347 to A.D. 1527**, running through 17 sultans over 182 years — a dynasty founded by Allauddin Hasan Gangu at Gulbarga in defiance of a weakening Delhi Sultanate, and one that ended, after Kareemulla's nominal reign, in the rise of five independent successor kingdoms: Barid Shahi (Bidar), Qutub Shahi (Golconda), Adil Shahi (Bijapur), Nizam Shahi (Ahmadnagar), and Imad Shahi (Berar). 

Its internal politics were often turbulent — several sultans were murdered, deposed, or blinded — even as the dynasty fought its long, unresolved contest with Vijayanagara across the Krishna–Tungabhadra doab. Prime Ministers like Mahmud Gavan strengthened administration and reformed the army and revenue system, while the Sufi philosophy, spread through figures such as Gesudaraj and reflected in the Deccan's wider Hindu–Muslim syncretism, carried Sufi teaching outward across the region. 

Under Bahamani rule, trade and commerce with Arabia, Persia, and East Africa expanded, and the rulers developed towns such as Firozabad while advancing regions like Bidar. Towns including Bidar, Raichur, Gulbarga, Daulatabad, Aurangabad, and Ahamadnagar became centres of Muslim development. 

In society, the division based on caste and class remained clearly visible, and the influence of Islam on Hindu religious life became increasingly predominant — overall, the Deccan became the stage for Islamic rule, culture, and architecture, and it was Bahamani rule that marked the beginning of the era of Muslim kingdoms in the Deccan.
